Q8294.L1t: Water's phase diagram shows the solid, liquid and gas regions separated by equilibrium lines that meet at a triple point.
Q8294.L2t: The liquid-solid equilibrium line of water slopes backward (up and to the left), unlike that of most substances, which slope forward.
Q8294.L3t: In ice, hydrogen bonds hold water molecules in an open, ordered crystalline lattice that packs them less densely than the liquid, so ice floats, and applying pressure favors the denser phase.
Q8294.L4t: The negative slope arises because ice is less dense than liquid water, owing to its hydrogen-bonded crystalline framework.
Q8294.L2f: The triple point of water lies at a pressure far above atmospheric pressure, so water at 1 atm can never exist as a gas.
Q8294.L3f: Solid water is less dense than liquid water, and it is low external pressure that pushes the solid to melt into liquid, which fixes the slope of the line.
Q8294.L4f: The negative slope is explained by ice being less dense than liquid water, which makes the solid turn into liquid under low pressure.

Q8245.L1t: Sensory psychology studies how stimuli are detected, and thresholds are measured by presenting stimuli of varying intensity and recording responses.
Q8245.L2t: An absolute threshold is conventionally defined as the minimum stimulus intensity that an organism detects 50% of the time.
Q8245.L3t: Of 30 mice, half is 15, and the power level at which exactly 15 mice pressed the lever is the one detected 50% of the time.
Q8245.L4t: The absolute threshold is the 70% power level, since that is where half of the mice responded.
Q8245.L2f: Absolute threshold is defined as the smallest stimulus intensity that a subject detects every single time it is presented.
Q8245.L3f: Defining the threshold requires a stimulus level and a response rate that cannot be matched to the data here, because the number of mice that could hear without the aid is not reported.
Q8245.L4f: There is not enough information given to identify the absolute threshold from these results.

Q5100.L1t: Landowners and landlords can be held liable in negligence for injuries on or near their property, depending on the duty they owe and the foreseeability of harm.
Q5100.L2t: A landlord's liability for a third party's criminal act generally depends on whether the landlord had a duty to protect and whether the harm was a foreseeable result of conditions they could control.
Q5100.L3t: The owner knew of the tenant's drug dealing and of earlier violent confrontations including a gun discharge, so a shooting that endangers neighbors was a foreseeable risk that the owner could have reduced by evicting.
Q5100.L4t: The neighbor should recover because the owner knew of the danger created by the tenant's drug dealing and did nothing about it.
Q5100.L2f: Courts treat landlords as having no responsibility at all for conditions arising from tenants' activities once the lease has been signed and rent is being paid.
Q5100.L3f: Merely knowing that a tenant deals drugs, without any knowledge of violence, is by itself enough to make a landlord strictly liable for any injury connected to that tenant.
Q5100.L4f: The neighbor should recover simply because the owner knew that the tenant was dealing drugs from his apartment.
